title: Deck Builder Invoice Template
subtitle: An invoice pre-filled for deck construction — decking, framing, labor, railing and stain. Download as Excel (auto-calculating), Word, or PDF.
taxHint: Look up your state's sales tax rate
paymentTerms: Net 14 — payment due within 14 days. Late fee of 1.5% per month applies after the due date.
notes: Thank you for your business. All deck work performed per local code and load requirements.
features: Auto-calculating tax formulas in Excel (just enter your state rate)
Pre-filled deck line items: decking, framing, labor, railing, stain
License # and EIN / Tax ID fields — required on client-facing invoices in most states
Materials and labor broken out with railing and stain as separate lines

faqs.q: What should I include on a deck builder invoice?
faqs.a: At minimum: your business and contractor license number, the client and job-site address, a dated line-item list (decking, framing, labor, railing, stain), tax, and total due. Note load rating and footing depth per local code.

faqs.q: Is this template free to use?
faqs.a: Yes. All three formats (PDF, Word, Excel) are free to download with no email required.

faqs.q: Does the Excel version calculate tax automatically?
faqs.a: Yes. Enter your quantity and rate per line, and the subtotal, tax and total update automatically. Leave the tax rate blank if you are not required to charge sales tax.

faqs.q: Is this legal or tax advice?
faqs.a: No. Templates are for informational purposes only. Requirements vary by state — verify with your contractor board and a CPA or attorney before use.

faqs.q: How do you estimate a deck: per square foot or by material takeoff?
faqs.a: Both, for different purposes. Square-foot pricing ($35 to $60 per square foot installed for a typical pressure-treated deck) is what customers compare, so use it for the first conversation. The actual estimate should be a material takeoff — joists, decking boards, posts, concrete, hangers, fasteners — because that is where the real cost lives and where a square-foot price silently loses money on a tall, small-footprint or multi-level deck.

faqs.q: What hidden costs should appear on a deck estimate?
faqs.a: Footings are the most common omission: concrete, excavation, and inspection can add $1,000 to $4,000 depending on frost depth and how many posts need to go below grade. Others: stairs and railing priced per linear foot rather than included in the platform rate, ledger flashing and waterproofing against the house, permits, and disposal of demolition debris. Each belongs on its own line, not absorbed into the decking price.

faqs.q: How do I price deck railing and stairs?
faqs.a: Per linear foot of railing and per step for stairs, separately from the deck surface. Railing runs $40 to $120 per linear foot installed depending on material and whether code requires a specific infill pattern; stairs run $100 to $300 per step depending on rise, width and whether a landing is needed. Counting them as part of the deck square footage is how a deck estimate loses margin on anything that is not a simple rectangle.

faqs.q: Do I need a permit, and is it billed separately?
faqs.a: Almost every jurisdiction requires a permit for a deck above a certain height, and most require one regardless when the deck is attached to a dwelling. Bill the permit fee as a pass-through line and the time spent on drawings and inspection separately. The bigger issue is code: guard height, stair geometry and footing depth all vary, and an estimate that does not state which code edition it was priced to is a dispute waiting to happen.

faqs.q: What is a normal deposit for a deck build?
faqs.a: A material deposit of 25 to 40 percent on acceptance is standard, released before lumber is ordered, followed by a progress payment when framing is complete and the balance at final inspection. Special-order items — composite decking in a specific colour, custom railing — often need to be covered in full at order time because they cannot be returned. Show that on the estimate rather than surprising the customer at the deposit request.

faqs.q: How do I handle a deck estimate when the customer changes material mid-job?
faqs.a: Price changes as a written change order before the material is ordered, never after it is installed. Composite versus pressure-treated is the most common switch, and it changes material cost by a factor of two or more plus different fastener and gap requirements. Note on the original estimate that pricing assumes the material listed, and that substitutions are quoted separately.

deepDive.heading: Deck building invoices: board feet, footings and the inspection holdback
deepDive.sub: A deck is priced in square feet but built in footings, framing, boards and railings — each with its own permit and inspection consequence. Here is how to itemize a deck invoice so the customer sees what passed inspection and what did not.

blocks.h3: Price the deck in four layers, not one square-foot rate
paras: Deck builders quote per square foot for the surface, then discover that the footings, the framing and the railing carry as much labour as the decking itself. A 300 sq ft deck might be 60% framing, footings and railing and 40% boards, but the customer mentally divides the total by square footage and compares it to a neighbour's quote for a different design.

Break the estimate into four layers: footings and posts, framing and joists, decking surface, railing and stairs. Each layer has its own material and its own hours, and each is where a change order lives. When the customer adds stairs or swaps composite for cedar, you can reprice one layer instead of the whole job.
list: Footings: per footing, including excavation, concrete, inspection and post base
Framing: ledger, rim, joists, blocking, hangers — priced by linear foot or by piece
Decking surface: sq ft by material (pressure-treated, cedar, composite, PVC)
Railing and stairs: linear foot of railing, per-tread for stairs
Fascia and trim: often forgotten, always visible

blocks.h3: Footings and the inspection that stops the job
paras: Almost every deck needs a building permit, and the footing inspection happens before any concrete is poured. Frost depth varies from 12 inches in the south to 48 inches or more in northern states, and a footing that is too shallow will fail inspection after the hole has been dug. That inspection is a schedule event, not a line item, and it costs a day of the job.

Ledger attachment is the other inspection hotspot. Bolting a ledger to a house through siding without flashing, or through a brick veneer without a standoff, is the most commonly failed deck inspection in the country. Estimate the flashing, the standoffs and the correct structural screws as their own material — and state on the invoice that the ledger attachment was inspected and approved.
list: Footing depth to local frost line — check before quoting, not after digging
Ledger flashing and standoffs are code, not optional upgrades
Inspection milestones: footing, framing, final
Post bases and hardware rated for ground contact and treated lumber

blocks.h3: Composite vs wood changes the material number and the customer conversation
paras: Composite decking costs two to three times pressure-treated per square foot, is typically sold by the linear foot of board rather than square footage, and needs specific fastener clips and a matching fascia. It also expands and contracts more, which sets the gap and the picture-frame detail. If you quote composite at the pressure-treated rate, you lose money on the biggest line in the job.

Cedar and other natural woods need staining, and staining is maintenance the customer has to do. Put both the material specification and the required maintenance interval on the estimate. A customer choosing composite for low maintenance should see that saving named on the invoice — it justifies the higher number they are being asked to approve.
list: Board sizing: 5/4x6 nominal is 1 inch by 5.5 inch actual — price by actual coverage
Hidden fastener clips and edge screws per board type
Stain or seal: cedar and pressure-treated both need it; composite does not
Warranty: composite has a manufacturer warranty, wood has yours

blocks.h3: Railing, stairs and the code items nobody budgets
paras: Railing is priced per linear foot and carries several code requirements: a maximum 4-inch gap between balusters, a 36-inch minimum height for residential, and a graspable handrail profile on stairs. Stairs are priced per tread and need their own stringers, footings and landing. These are not extras — they are code, and a deck without them fails final inspection.

Two more items that catch customers out: the deck's lateral load connection to the house (a modern requirement in most jurisdictions) and the framing inspection before decking goes on. Both belong in the estimate as named scope, because a customer who was not told about a $400 hardware kit and an extra inspection day will not pay for them at the end without an argument.
list: Railing: linear feet, baluster spacing to code, graspable handrail on stairs
Stairs: per tread plus stringers, landing and footing
Lateral load connection hardware — required in most jurisdictions, frequently omitted
Framing inspection before decking: a schedule day, not a cost line

blocks.h3: Payment terms that protect a deck job
paras: Deck jobs are front-loaded with material: lumber, concrete, hardware and railing arrive before the first board is laid. A schedule of 30 to 40 percent on contract signing, a progress payment when framing is inspected, and the balance on final inspection is standard. Holding the final payment until the final inspection passes aligns both sides — the customer has a finished deck, and you have proof that it passed.

Put the permit and inspection status on every invoice: permit number, inspections passed and their dates. If a customer sells the house two years later and the buyer's inspector asks for the deck permit, that invoice is the one document that proves the deck was built legally.
list: Deposit at signing for materials; progress after framing inspection; balance after final
Permit number and inspection dates printed on the invoice
Change orders numbered and signed before the change is built
State the warranty: structure vs finish are usually different periods
